Thank you for submitting your article "Distinct mechanisms of microRNA sorting into cancer cell-derived extracellular vesicle subtypes" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor (Suzanne Pfeffer) and Jeffrey Settleman as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission. One of the reviewers has included a number of very detailed comments that should be easily addressed.

Summary:

The present study by Temoche-Diaz et al., reports that Lupus La protein packages a subset of miRNAs for export in a subset of endosome-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs). The authors used ultracentrifugation followed by iodixanol-based centrifugation to obtain two biochemically distinct "EV subtypes" (LD and HD) in which they find different, significantly enriched miRNAs. The authors further provide evidence that La binds miR-122 (specifically enriched in HD EVs) to mediate its targeting within exosomes. Using a semi-reconstituted cell-free assay and binding experiments the authors conclude that La specifically engages a subset of microRNAs in the exosome biogenesis pathway. The work will be of broad interest if the authors can determine the number of miRNAs that depend on La for their packaging. Also, a recently published paper should be discussed in relation to the current story.

Jeppesen et al., 2019 analyzed different cell types (including the MDA-MB-231 cell line) using a similar approach to isolate two distinct fractions, LD and HD. Jeppesen et al., extended their analysis by including IPs using specific tetraspanins (CD63, CD81, CD9) to further isolate vesicles from non-vesicular particles (exomeres, lipoproteins and other RNA-binding protein complexes), the latter found to be mostly enriched in the HD fraction. Their data on CD63 versus CD9 seem to differ from the present story but could this be a cell-type dependent effect? This must be answered.

Previous work by Schekman and colleagues also used anti-CD63 immunoprecipitation to isolate vesicles enriched for microRNAs. La protein can interact with major vault protein (MVP)-particles (Kickhoefer et al., 2002), an RNA-binding proteinaceous organelle that has previously been shown to be export microRNAs by poorly understood mechanisms (Jeppesen et al., 2019, Teng et al., 2017). Vault particles were enriched in Coffey's iodixanol HD fractions of MDA-MB-231 cells.

Essential revisions:

1) Jeppesen et al., clearly showed that while their "LDs" are almost exclusively enriched in vesicles, the predominant components of the HD fraction are non-vesicular structures. Thus it would be important for the authors to show that miR-122 is detected in anti-CD63 immuno-isolated vesicles from the HD fraction, and that miR-122 export is dependent on Rab27A. Figure 6C shows a sucrose flotation performed on isolated HD iodixanol fractions, which is consistent with these authors' conclusion, but anti-CD63 IP would add a lot.

2) The authors should blot for an additional non-vesicular particle marker (MVP or Ago?) for their Optiprep gradient fractions. The blots for CD63 or TSG101 are rather smeary across these fractions. Typically, CD63 runs as a smear due to glycosylation and only a few antibodies work on gels run under reducing conditions. Please provide molecular weight markers for the blots and consider whether your antibody is appropriately recognizing CD63 as it seems to have a strange pattern (2 discrete bands) and to be present across the whole blot, not really enriched in any fractions. Jeppesen et al., showed Ago1 and Ago2 in the HD fraction of MDA-MB-231 cells. Please at least discuss this parallel study in relation to the current findings.

3) Does depletion of La protein change the overall miRNA signature of the LD and HD fractions? This would provide important information as to how many miRNAs rely on the proposed La pathway for export and would add much to the significance of the present story.

4) Immunoprecipitated La in Figure 7 may co-immunoprecipitate vault proteins (MVPs), which may also be needed for export of miR-122. The authors should show in Figure 8 the non-binding miRNA sequence for comparison.

5) It is not clear that Rab27a-KO is really making the HD population go away – please show this with a density gradient analysis, with quantitation of vesicle numbers and Western blot analysis of the gradient fractions. It also seems strange that the HD fraction and not the LD fraction would go away with Rab27a KO unless the method you use here is much different from that used in Kowal et al. in which the LD fraction was thought to represent exosomes. Please clarify.

results.result: Two biochemically distinct small extracellular vesicle (sEV) sub-populations, termed vLD (low density, 1.09-1.11 g/ml) and vHD (high density, 1.14-1.16 g/ml), were separated from MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells using buoyant density gradient centrifugation. These sub-populations exhibit differential protein marker distribution (CD9 enriched in vLD, CD63 enriched in vHD), distinct subcellular localizations (CD9 at plasma membrane, CD63 in endosomes), and different biogenesis pathways (vHD secretion is Rab27a-dependent, vLD is not), suggesting vHD vesicles originate from the endocytic pathway while vLD vesicles bud from the plasma membrane.
results.evaluation: The separation of two sEV sub-populations is well-supported by multiple orthogonal lines of evidence: buoyant density measurements (C52, C55), nanoparticle tracking analysis showing overlapping but distinct size distributions (C48-C51), differential protein marker distribution by immunoblot and mass spectrometry (C45, C53-C59), immunofluorescence showing distinct subcellular localizations (C60-C63), and genetic perturbation experiments with Rab27a and Rab35 knockouts demonstrating differential biogenesis requirements (C66-C75). The conclusion about different subcellular origins (C64, C76, C77) is a reasonable inference from the combined biochemical, proteomic, and genetic data.

results.result: The vHD and vLD sEV sub-populations utilize fundamentally different miRNA sorting mechanisms. The vHD sub-population employs selective miRNA sorting, with 21 miRNAs enriched ≥10-fold compared to cellular levels (50-1000-fold enrichment by qPCR), while the vLD sub-population shows non-selective or minimal selective miRNA sorting (0.5-5-fold enrichment). This was validated using two orthogonal profiling methods (Firefly and TGIRT-seq) and confirmed by RNase protection assays demonstrating vesicle encapsulation.
results.evaluation: The differential miRNA sorting mechanisms are robustly supported by convergent evidence from multiple profiling platforms (Firefly: C81-C88; TGIRT-seq: C89-C95) showing consistent patterns of high enrichment in vHD but not vLD. The validation by RT-qPCR (C102-C109) confirms the profiling results with quantitative measurements. RNase protection assays (C112-C113) demonstrate bona fide vesicle encapsulation rather than surface association. The conclusion of selective vs. non-selective sorting (C110-C111, C114) is well-justified by the magnitude and specificity of enrichment differences between the two populations.

results.result: The Lupus La protein mediates selective sorting of miR-122 into vesicles, as demonstrated by in vitro packaging assays. La-depleted cytosol showed ~4-fold reduced miR-122 packaging efficiency, which was rescued by addition of purified recombinant La protein. The sorting of La bound to miR-122 requires membranes, cytosol, and physiological temperature (30°C), and La alone is insufficient without additional cytosolic factors.
results.evaluation: The role of La in miR-122 packaging is well-established through multiple complementary experiments: depletion-rescue experiments showing La-dependence (C139, C147-C148), specificity demonstrated by YBX1-independence (C128-C129), mass spectrometry identification (C131), and co-isolation experiments showing temperature and component requirements (C151-C152). The rescue with purified La protein (C148) provides strong evidence for direct involvement rather than indirect effects. The requirement for additional cytosolic factors (C149-C150) is appropriately acknowledged as a limitation.

results.result: La protein is required for selective miRNA sorting into sEVs in vivo. CRISPRi-mediated La depletion caused 2.7-fold intracellular accumulation of miR-122 and significant reduction in its secretion into sEVs, without affecting total sEV numbers or non-selectively sorted miRNAs. All tested selectively sorted miRNAs showed ≥50% reduction in secretion upon La depletion, while non-selectively sorted miRNAs were unaffected. La protein was detected in the vHD fraction and is encapsulated within sEVs as demonstrated by proteinase K protection assays.
results.evaluation: The in vivo role of La is strongly supported by genetic perturbation experiments showing specific effects on selectively sorted miRNAs (C154, C157, C159-C160) without affecting vesicle biogenesis (C156) or non-selective sorting (C155, C160). The detection of La in vHD vesicles by immunoblot (C162-C163) and proteinase K protection (C166) confirms its presence as a bona fide cargo. The breadth of effect across multiple selectively sorted miRNAs (C159) strengthens the conclusion of a general sorting mechanism rather than miRNA-specific effects.

results.result: Two sequence motifs in miR-122 are responsible for high-affinity binding to La protein and sorting into vesicles: a 3' UUU motif and a 5' UGGA motif. The La:miR-122 complex has a Kd of 4.8 nM, which is higher affinity than Ago2-miRNA interactions (10-80 nM). Mutation of the 3' UUU motif reduced binding affinity ~100-fold (Kd 538 nM) and packaging efficiency to 3% (vs. 15% for WT), while mutation of the 5' UGGA motif reduced affinity ~10-fold and impaired packaging. The UGGA motif was identified by MEME analysis as enriched in vHD miRNAs (26% vs. 5% in cellular miRNAs).
results.evaluation: The bipartite motif requirement is well-supported by convergent evidence from multiple approaches: EMSA showing quantitative binding affinity measurements (C179-C180, C185), in vitro packaging assays demonstrating functional consequences of mutations (C184, C193), and unbiased motif discovery by MEME analysis (C188-C192). The magnitude of effects (100-fold for 3' motif, 10-fold for 5' motif) correlates with functional importance. The comparison to Ago2 affinity (C180) provides important context. The conclusion of a bipartite recognition mechanism (C195) is well-justified by the additive effects of mutating both motifs.

results.result: Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed that La protein is present in both nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments in MDA-MB-231 cells. Most cytoplasmic La localizes to punctate structures smaller than ~100 nm, with larger La structures (>500 nm) showing co-localization with the late endosomal marker Rab7.
results.evaluation: The subcellular localization of La is directly demonstrated by immunofluorescence (C174) with appropriate controls showing antibody specificity. The observation of La puncta co-localizing with Rab7 (C176, C245) is consistent with the proposed role in endosome-derived vesicle biogenesis and provides spatial context for the sorting mechanism. The size distribution of La puncta (C175, C244) is appropriately characterized.

results.result: Ago2 and Dicer are not present in purified sEVs from MDA-MB-231 cells. Both proteins are detected in the crude high-speed pellet but do not float with vesicles in buoyant density gradients, indicating they are associated with non-vesicular RNP complexes that co-sediment during ultracentrifugation.
results.evaluation: The absence of Ago2 and Dicer from purified sEVs is clearly demonstrated by immunoblot analysis across density gradients (C46, C134-C135) and is consistent with previous studies using stringent purification methods (C47, C137). This finding is important for interpreting the mechanism of selective miRNA sorting and challenges assumptions about RISC involvement in EV-mediated miRNA transfer. The conclusion that these proteins are in non-vesicular RNPs (C136) is a reasonable inference from their sedimentation but not flotation behavior.

results.result: MDA-MB-231 cells actively secrete miR-122, as demonstrated by time-course experiments showing accumulation of miR-122 in conditioned media over 48 hours in the presence of cells but not in cell-free media. miR-122 co-fractionates specifically with the vHD fraction in iodixanol gradients, separated from non-vesicular RNPs.
results.evaluation: The active secretion of miR-122 by MDA-MB-231 cells is well-demonstrated by the time-course experiment (C118-C119) which controls for pre-existing miR-122 in serum. The co-fractionation with vHD vesicles (C121-C122) confirms vesicle association and is consistent with the selective sorting mechanism. This result provides important validation that the in vitro findings are relevant to cellular miR-122 secretion.

results.result: Non-selective miRNA sorting occurs in both vHD and vLD sub-populations, with slight enrichment in vHD and minor depletion in vLD. The authors propose this may correlate with the cytoplasmic pool of RISC-free miRNAs, as Ago2 and Dicer are absent from purified sEVs. The differential distribution may reflect proximity to endosomes (vHD) versus plasma membrane (vLD) biogenesis sites.
results.evaluation: While the observation of non-selective sorting is supported by data (C198-C200), the mechanistic explanations are largely speculative (C201, C205-C206, C210). The hypothesis about RISC-free miRNAs is reasonable given the absence of Ago2/Dicer (C204) and literature on variable RISC association (C202), but lacks direct experimental validation. The proposed spatial model (C210) is plausible but not tested. This represents an interesting hypothesis requiring further investigation rather than a well-supported conclusion.

results.result: tRNAs are the most abundant small non-coding transcripts in both vHD (88.6%) and vLD (96.3%) sEV sub-populations. Most tRNA reads start at position 16, likely representing a reverse transcription stop at an unidentified EV-enriched D-loop modification previously described. Both sEV sub-populations share this modified tRNA species.
results.evaluation: The abundance of tRNAs in both sEV populations is clearly demonstrated by TGIRT-seq data (C96-C98) and is consistent with previous findings (C215). The start position analysis (C99) provides evidence for a shared modification, though the exact nature remains unidentified (C100). The conclusion that both populations share modified tRNA sorting machinery (C217) is speculative but reasonable given the similar enrichment patterns (C216). This is a well-characterized observation though the mechanistic implications remain unclear.

results.result: Current sEV isolation methods co-isolate multiple EV species and do not separate sEVs from non-vesicular protein and RNA-protein complexes. Previous studies showing selective miRNA sorting in sEVs may have been confounded by heterogeneous sub-populations, as the sEV fraction was not further purified.
results.evaluation: This critical assessment of the field is well-supported by the authors' own data demonstrating sEV heterogeneity and by citations to relevant literature (C17-C22). The specific critique of the Tosar et al. study (C31-C32) is a reasonable interpretation that motivates the current work. This represents appropriate contextualization of prior work and justification for the current study's approach.

results.result: Tumor cells can simultaneously deploy multiple EV species using distinct sorting mechanisms (selective in vHD, non-selective in vLD), which may enable diverse functions in cancer biology. The distinct miRNA compositions of vHD and vLD sub-populations could explain differential effects on gene expression in recipient cells observed in previous studies.
results.evaluation: While the observation of multiple EV species with distinct sorting mechanisms is well-supported (C11, C196-C197), the functional implications are largely speculative (C12, C222). The connection to diverse functions in cancer biology is proposed but not experimentally tested in this study. The reference to differential gene expression effects (C220-C221) from other work provides some support, but the causal link to miRNA composition remains unproven. This represents an important hypothesis for future work rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: The role of La in miRNA sorting may extend to other cell types, as B cell-derived sEVs are enriched for 3' uridylylated miRNAs and La has been detected in B cell EVs. However, different cell types may use different RNA-binding proteins for selective sorting, as SYNCRIP (required in hepatocytes) was not detected in the MDA-MB-231 system. The process may be organized by cell-specific assembly of RNA granules.
results.evaluation: The generalizability of La-mediated sorting is supported by circumstantial evidence from B cells (C235-C236) but lacks direct experimental validation in other cell types (C234). The observation that SYNCRIP is absent in MDA-MB-231 cells (C238) supports cell-type specificity (C239) but this is based on negative data. The proposals about high-affinity interactions (C240-C241) and RNA granule organization (C243) are speculative. This represents reasonable extrapolation from the data but requires experimental validation in other systems.

results.result: The functional significance of EV-mediated miRNA transfer in cancer remains uncertain. While many studies suggest EVs promote metastasis through miRNA transfer, the absence of Ago2 in purified EVs raises questions about how transferred miRNAs would function in recipient cells. Alternative mechanisms such as selective disposal of tumor suppressor miRNAs are also possible.
results.evaluation: This represents a critical assessment of the field rather than a specific result from the current study. The observation that highly-selected miRNAs are not bound to Ago2 (C251) is well-supported and raises important mechanistic questions (C252-C253). However, the functional implications remain speculative, with both intercellular communication (C246-C249) and disposal mechanisms (C254-C256) being plausible but unproven (C257). The critique of current evidence (C261, C263) is valid but does not resolve the functional question. This highlights an important gap in the field requiring future investigation.
